strengths: The main technical contribution of the paper is a generalization of an existing framework from functions with a Lipschitz continuous gradient to the case of differentiable functions.
A non negligible contribution in my opinion is the very clear presentation with several interesting remarks.
The assumptions and the statements are clear and the proofs technically sound.
The presentation is good. The authors provide solid theoretical analysis to support the proposed framework.
This paper is generally well-written and easy to follow. It is well-grounded in theoretical analysis, establishing convergence guarantees without relying on smoothness assumptions.
It unifies multiple SPPM variants under a single theoretical framework, making it easier to understand the relationships and convergence behavior across methods.
The development of new SPPM variants, such as SPPM with Nonuniform Sampling and SPPM with Arbitrary Sampling, enriches the field by expanding the applicability of SPPM.
The proposed universal SPPM algorithmic framework sounds interesting, and novel as far as the reviewer knows about.
The convergence analysis is generally well presented, with sufficient details provided in a clear and neat way in the appendix sections.
weaknesses: The idea is not new and is a generalization of existing approaches, limiting novelty.
The novelty of the contribution is limited.
The title is misleading since analysis only covers smooth (differentiable) functions, while nonsmooth ones are not covered.
Assumption 5 involves unknown quantities; it is unclear how more general it is in practice and concrete examples are needed to establish impact.
The claim that a unifying framework for variance reduction techniques is missing is false because existing papers already provide such frameworks.
Algorithm 1 is the universal one that includes all other algorithms, reducing distinct contributions.
SPPM* and SPPM GC are not practically interesting because they require gradients at the solution.
The motivation of this paper is unclear.
The assumption without smoothness used in this paper looks not popular.

The paper appears more like a review article, which may not align well with the scope of ICLR; the proposed seven algorithms may lack sufficient novelty or clear performance advantages, leaving readers uncertain about the best choice.
The framework assumes strong convexity, limiting applicability to problems that are not strongly convex or to non-convex settings.
Algorithm 1 uses a constant, sufficiently small step size, which is rarely practical; a diminishing step size would be more effective and should be discussed.

The authors claim to use a weaker assumption (without smoothness) but their experiments consider a convex least squares problem that satisfies the smoothness assumption; an example violating the ν-smoothness assumption is needed.
The empirical experiments are limited to strongly convex least squares problems, restricting relevance to practical applications and broader research interests.

The main result in Theorem 1 has a bound that seems non-vanishing with respect to time unless certain constants are zero; an adaptive bound for standard SPPM with sublinear convergence would be more interesting.
Experiments are limited to toy linear regression problems with very limited data scale.
It would be more desirable to test the proposed algorithms on non-smooth learning tasks such as SVMs with hinge loss.
